The market added six billion dollars in value. Mark Zuckerberg personally gained one point one billion dollars in a single day. The punishment made the company richer than if the government had done nothing.

segments.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto that was rear-ended in San Bernardino. The fuel tank ruptured. The driver burned to death. Richard survived — barely. Burned over his entire body. Lost parts of his fingers. Lost his left ear. Years of skin grafts. A childhood replaced by hospital rooms. The jury awarded one hundred and twenty-five million dollars in punitive damages — the largest in American history. The judge reduced it to three point five million. Ford was acquitted of criminal homicide. No executive went to prison.

segments.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous. She told the truth. She'd watched her colleagues at Wells Fargo open accounts that customers never asked for — credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist, savings accounts funded by moving money between other accounts without permission. She knew why they did it. There was a quota: every customer should have eight products. "Eight is Great." Miss the number and you get a warning. Miss it again and you get fired. So the tellers cheated. Because the alternative was unemployment.

You couldn't find it by browsing Reddit. You couldn't stumble on it. The only way to reach it was through a crawler. It was bait. A tripwire designed to catch one thing: an AI company scraping Reddit's content without permission.

segments.text: When Ford got caught, they could recall the car. When Facebook got caught, they could — in theory — delete the data. When Purdue got caught, they could stop manufacturing the pills. The damage was reversible. Expensive, slow, and nobody ever did it voluntarily. But the off switch existed.

segments.text: With AI, there is no off switch. When a model trains on scraped data, that data dissolves into the model's parameters like sugar dissolved in water. You cannot un-dissolve it. You cannot identify which outputs came from which inputs. You cannot point to a sentence and say "that came from Reddit" or "that came from a children's book published in 2019." The data becomes the model. The violation becomes the product. Every response the AI generates, every image it creates, every answer it provides — built on content taken without permission and impossible to return.

beats.text: With AI, there is no off switch.

segments.text: Elliana is an illustrator in Charlotte, North Carolina. Self-taught. She spent years building a career in minimalistic line work — psychological, introspective, distinctive. The kind of art you'd recognize on a bookshelf. She illustrated covers for HarperCollins, Little Brown, and Faber and Faber. She designed album art for Universal Music Group. She created promotional work for Hulu. Art was her full-time job for four years. She'd built something.

The style she'd spent a decade developing could now be approximated in seconds by typing a sentence into a box. She started pivoting to 3D art — not because she wanted to, but because she hoped three-dimensional work would be harder to scrape.

segments.text: Chris Vialpondo is a renter in Seattle's Lower Queen Anne neighborhood. In 2022, he opened a notice from his property manager and learned his rent had increased by fifty percent. Same apartment. Same neighborhood. Same job. He was already working two jobs to make rent. Fifty percent meant the difference between getting by and going under. It meant counting every grocery trip. It meant the constant math of which bill gets paid this week and which one waits. He reached out to his property manager — the human being he thought had set the price — and was told nothing could be done. Because his property manager hadn't set the price. A company he'd never heard of had.

segments.text: RealPage. A company that takes confidential pricing data from competing landlords — data that competitors are not legally supposed to share — and feeds it into an algorithm that recommends rent prices across more than thirteen million apartments. Ninety percent of landlords follow the recommendation. The result: coordinated rent increases across buildings that are supposed to be competing with each other. The Department of Justice found that the algorithm costs renters an average of seventy dollars a month more — and over a hundred dollars a month in six major metro areas.

segments.text: Europe figured this out. Four percent of global revenue. Proportional. Automatic. No ceiling. When the fine scales with the company, the formula breaks. Facebook shrugged off a five-billion-dollar American fine and panicked over a European one. The tools exist. Criminal liability for executives — not the tellers, the architects. Disgorgement — hand back every dollar earned from the violation, not a negotiated fraction. The legal frameworks are built. The question has never been how. The question is why.

That's what the GDPR did to data privacy.
That's what proportional fines could do to corporate crime.
The question isn't whether the formula can be broken. It already has been — in pockets.
The question is whether America wants to break it.

segments.text: The Sackler name is still on a wing of the Guggenheim Museum in New York City. The Metropolitan Museum took theirs down after public outcry. The Guggenheim hasn't. You can walk into one of the most prestigious cultural institutions in the world, look up at the wall, and read the name of a family that earned their fortune from a drug that killed eight hundred thousand people. They kept thirteen billion. And they kept the wall.

beats.text: The Sackler name is still on a wing of the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.
The Metropolitan Museum took theirs down.
But the name remains at Harvard, Tufts, and Oxford.

segments.notes: Two internal beat markers = brief pauses between the three institutions. Neutral/measured tone — quiet outrage, not screaming. The contrast between Met (took it down) and Guggenheim/Harvard (didn't) is the argument. Settlement imagery for Harvard/Oxford = institutional legitimacy protecting the name.

segments.text: That's the formula. It even gets you a plaque.

beats.text: That's the formula.

segments.notes: Beat + 3s pause after — this is the punchline of the entire Sackler section. Silence does more work than SFX here. Museum plaque detail shot on 'It even gets you a plaque' is the visual match. 3s hold lets it breathe before moving to Esquivel.

segments.text: Elliana Esquivel is still making art in Charlotte. She pivoted to 3D — not because she chose to, but because the alternative was watching her style get reproduced for free. If the settlement arrives, her share might cover a month of rent. The model keeps running.

beats.text: Elliana Esquivel is still making art in Charlotte.
She pivoted to 3D — not because she chose to, but because the alternatives — licensing her images to AI, watching them train anyway, trying to compete — all felt like losing.

segments.text: Seventy-four percent of Facebook users still don't know the platform profiles them. The data harvested in 2014 was never deleted. The models built on it were refined.

beats.text: Seventy-four percent of Facebook users still don't know the platform profiles them.
The data harvested in 2014 was never deleted.
And the formula worked — because it keeps working.

Stat overlay surfaces the 74% ignorance number. Shimmer on the thesis line creates an unsettled, open-ended feeling — the formula is still running as this video plays.

segments.text: Chris Vialpondo is still in Seattle. Still working two jobs. The algorithm that raised his rent is still running. His fifty percent increase was not a market decision. It was a formula.

beats.text: Chris Vialpondo is still in Seattle. Still working two jobs.

His fight is ongoing.

segments.notes: Callback to Vialpondo — the human cost the whole video built toward. Three RealPage-specific images matched beat-by-beat to the VO. Somber, measured. The algorithm visual on 'still running' is the editorial gut punch.

segments.text: The Grush-Saunby memo put a dollar value on a human life in 1977. Two hundred thousand dollars. Purdue's settlement valued each opioid death at nine thousand. Facebook's fine valued each compromised user at fifty-seven dollars. The AI settlements value each stolen book at three thousand dollars. Elliana's illustrations? Not priced yet. Your Reddit posts? Your YouTube comments? Your blog from 2016?

beats.text: The Grush-Saunby memo put a dollar value on a human life in 1977. Two hundred thousand dollars.
Purdue's settlement valued each opioid death at...

segments.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.
